[{"role": "user", "content": "Why do vehicles that carry a lot of people not require seatbelts?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You've probably got it backwards a little. You'd be hard pressed to find a car, truck or van that lets a bunch of people ride around without belts. The big exception is the school bus and that's down to the way they are put together. The seats are built high and set close together so that a kid can't get very far in a crash. That whole arrangement is called compartmentalization and it ends up keeping people pretty well in place. You'd actually be in more danger if a child got up and got thrown around. That said it all falls apart once you get to college age or start looking at the rules in other countries.

You may be remembering the old style buses that didn't have that kind of protection. Those are almost all gone by now. It's really just a trade off between the physical protection the bus gives and the fact that getting a room full of small children to buckle up is next to impossible."}, {"role": "user", "content": "You said it "falls apart" for older riders or other countries. Can you give me one concrete example, like a specific country or US state that requires seatbelts on buses, and what the actual rule says?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "California is a good one to look at. The rule is that you have to have the kids buckled in if the bus is going to take a trip that crosses a state line. For the usual local runs to and from the school the old compartmentalization idea is still good enough. The whole thing exists mostly to stop a bus from some other state from coming in and running under its own looser rules. You end up with the destination state's requirements applying to the trip. You'll see a lot of the same sort of thing in the Canadian provinces too, though they each write it out a bit differently.

I can't give you the exact code section number off the top of my head and I'd rather not make one up. If you want to see the wording for yourself you can find it in the California Vehicle Code under the school bus provisions. It's not buried in some obscure sub paragraph."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Can you rewrite the compartmentalization explanation for a parent who's worried about their kid's safety, in plain terms without the jargon? Also, I thought California requires lap-shoulder belts on all new school buses, not just interstate trips, so double-check that before you write it."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You are mostly right and I was too neat in the first answer. California has been requiring the full lap and shoulder belts on new school buses for a while now. The old arrangement is still allowed on the older stuff that is already out there. So a kid on a brand new bus is going to get the belt while the one on an older one is not. You would need to look at the actual purchase date of the bus to know which is in effect.

For the part about how the old system works you can think of it this way. The seats are so high and so close together that a child just cannot get very far. If the bus stops all of a sudden the seat in front of the kid is going to stop the kid. That is the whole of the protection. You are trading the certainty of a belt for that arrangement. It works out for small children, it stops working out as they get bigger and the gaps between the seats stop being a barrier to them. That is the part that is going to worry you as your kid gets older."}, {"role": "user", "content": "For a while now" doesn't tell me anything: what's the actual cutoff year, and is it based on when the bus was manufactured or when the district bought it? Also, was the interstate-trip rule you mentioned earlier just wrong, or is that a separate thing that still exists?"}]
samples.reply:
You are right to push on that. The date that matters is the one stamped on the bus when it rolled off the line. A district that buys that bus two or three years later is still stuck with the rules that applied to that model year. You are not going to get any leeway from the purchase date. I can't give you the exact year the change got going though. It has been a slow phase in over a number of years rather than a single switch, and I would rather leave that out than get the number wrong.

You can also throw out that interstate trip business. That was me trying to explain something that does not actually work that way. The belts are a function of the bus it self and not of the route it happens to be on. A bus that is fully equipped is going to have to keep that equipment no matter what state it drives into. I mixed up two separate things there and you were right to call it out.

You are right to push on that since the two rules do get mixed up. The in state rule for new buses is a separate thing from the rules that hit a bus when it crosses a state line. I don't have a straight cutoff year to give you and I won't guess at one. What matters is the date the bus was first put into service, which is not quite the same as the date the district paid for it. A district can buy a used bus that was first used somewhere else and that earlier date is the one that counts. You would have to look at that first use date to see which set of rules the bus has to follow.

The California Department of Transportation keeps a fairly clear writeup of all this on its school bus safety pages. That is the only place you are going to get the exact dates that apply to the buses your kid is riding on.

samples.history: [{"role": "user", "content": "Are vitamin pills beneficial for us to take, or are they a complete waste of money? Is eating healthy food the only real way to absorb nutrients?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You'll get most of what you need from a decent diet and that's the route your body handles best. The other stuff in the whole food helps it get to work. That said you are going to run up against a few hard limits. You aren't going to get enough d from food alone unless you get a lot of sun. You are also going to miss out on some of the b vitamins if you are on a very strict vegetarian or vegan diet. You might also need to add in some iron if you are prone to anemia. Outside of those sorts of specific gaps the extra pills you are taking are probably just going to end up in the toilet. You are not going to get any extra benefit from taking massive doses of the things you are already getting in sufficient amounts."}, {"role": "user", "content": "I don't really buy the \"probably ends up in the toilet\" part, since my mom's 72 and her doctor has her on B12 and calcium because she doesn't absorb them well anymore. Can you rewrite the bit about who actually needs supplements so it's aimed at older adults like her?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "That is a pretty good example of where the whole thing starts to make sense. You are mostly in the same boat up to your fifties, but the gut gets worse at its job as you get older. You make less stomach acid and that makes it hard to split B12 off the proteins it comes attached to. You end up needing to take it in a form your body can pick up without that first step. You get into the same fix with calcium. The skin also stops making nearly as much D so you have to make up the difference. None of that is going to be much of a problem for a lot of people under 50. For the rest of the vitamin parade you are still mostly just paying to get rid of it."}, {"role": "user", "content": "You said calcium is \"the same fix\" as B12, but I doubt that, because B12 is about stomach acid freeing it from protein, and I thought calcium was more about vitamin D and bone loss after menopause. Is calcium actually absorbed the same way, or did you lump them together?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You are right to call that out, I got the two muddled together. The end result is the same in that you have to take it from the outside. The reason you have to is not. With the B12 you are stuck because the stomach has stopped making the acid needed to split it from the meat it is attached to. The calcium thing is a separate animal. You need the D to get it across the gut wall in the first place and then you are trying to keep up with the accelerated bone loss that hits after menopause. It just so happens that both of those problems tend to show up in the same set of people."}, {"role": "user", "content": "You said both have to be \"taken from the outside,\" but that's confusing: does that mean my mom needs the calcium pill itself, or is the real issue that she's low on D and can't absorb the calcium she already eats? Should she be taking D along with the calcium, or is the calcium alone enough?"}]
samples.reply: You almost certainly need both. Piling on more of the calcium is not going to get it across the gut wall if the D that does that job is missing. You are not going to get much in the way of a result from the calcium alone in that situation. That is the sort of thing that a simple blood test will sort out though. You are not going to get very far by guessing at which of the two is the actual shortcoming. The doctor she is already seeing should have no trouble running that. You will still have to keep up the B12 on top of all that as well. That one is not going to get fixed by sorting out the other two.

samples.reply: You are going to have to get that sorted out with the doctor. They can look at the blood work to see where the D is at. That will tell you whether the problem is mostly a lack of the helper or a lack of the mineral to begin with. You will not get that answer from a generic recommendation. That said it is hard to get the two entirely apart. If the D is missing the calcium she is already eating is going to pass right through. On the other hand the body has a pretty hard ceiling on how much it can pull in on any given day. If the diet is not putting in nearly enough the extra D is not going to make up for it. You end up having to supply the mineral in a more concentrated form as well.

It's the same problem you run into with a lot of stuff in life. You might notice that kids who wear glasses do worse on reading tests, but the glasses aren't what is messing up their eyes. Some other thing is behind both of those. The plastic in the plaque is in the same boat. You can see that the two things are hanging out together, you just can't yet say which way the arrows point. You can describe that block to the class in a way that gets the point across. You just have to be straight with them that you are generalizing from a lot of similar hits rather than pointing to one famous game.

Nobody is applying some deep grammatical rule that says little words are less important. You are just following a set of local agreements about what to call the main words. You keep the nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs in caps and you let the glue words slide. That contrast is what lets your eye pick out the important bits. If you capitalized everything you'd get a wall of equal emphasis that actually makes the thing harder to read.

You'll find the exact list of words to skip changes from one style manual to the next. The Chicago manual will have you capitalize the first and last word no matter what. The AP style is a bit more aggressive about lowercasing. You are really just following the particular set of local rules you have in front of you. A preposition can be the most important thing in a phrase and still get left in small letters."}, {"role": "user", "content": "If I want to auto-generate title case in code, how do libraries like Python's `titlecase` decide whether "up" in "Look Up Records" is a preposition or part of a phrasal verb? Or do they just lowercase it from a fixed stopword list and get it wrong?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You are almost certainly getting the second result. The library has a bag of words it has decided to leave in small letters and it will hit "up" with it every time. It has no idea that the word in front of it is making it act like a verb. You would have to get a part of speech tagger in there to get at that sort of thing. That gets you a long way but it is a fair bit slower and you will still get tripped up by the things the tagger itself misreads. You can get around it for the things you care about by keeping a separate list of the phrases that must be treated as a unit. You will just have to keep adding to that list as you run into new cases."}, {"role": "user", "content": "You mentioned a POS tagger. Would something like spaCy actually tag "up" in "Look Up Records" as a particle (RP) rather than a preposition (IN), given that title-cased input already throws off its casing cues?"}]
samples.reply:
You are right that the casing is a feature the model looks at. It keeps a running tally of things like whether a word is all caps or just initial caps, and that does feed into the decision. You are going to get a somewhat different feature vector out of "Look Up" than you would from "look up." That said the model has seen an awful lot of headlines in its training, so it isn't going to be completely lost by it.

In this particular case I would expect it to get it right. The pattern of a verb immediately followed by up is so strong that it will probably override the capital. You would be in more trouble with something like "Up in the Air" where the word is genuinely ambiguous. The model will just have to guess and you will get the answer it thinks is most likely. You are not going to get a hard guarantee either way.

You will also have to think about what it does with Records at the end. That one is easy enough since it is clearly a noun. The whole string is a bit of a stretch for the model to parse as it has no punctuation to work with.

Nobody is applying some deep grammatical rule that says little words are less important. You are just following a set of local agreements about what to call the main words. You keep the nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs in caps and you let the glue words slide. That contrast is what lets your eye pick out the important bits. If you capitalized everything you'd get a wall of equal emphasis that actually makes the thing harder to read.

You'll find the exact list of words to skip changes from one style manual to the next. The Chicago manual will have you capitalize the first and last word no matter what. The AP style is a bit more aggressive about lowercasing. You are really just following the particular set of local rules you have in front of you. A preposition can be the most important thing in a phrase and still get left in small letters."}, {"role": "user", "content": "If I want to auto-generate title case in code, how do libraries like Python's `titlecase` decide whether "up" in "Look Up Records" is a preposition or part of a phrasal verb? Or do they just lowercase it from a fixed stopword list and get it wrong?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You are almost certainly getting the second result. The library has a bag of words it has decided to leave in small letters and it will hit "up" with it every time. It has no idea that the word in front of it is making it act like a verb. You would have to get a part of speech tagger in there to get at that sort of thing. That gets you a long way but it is a fair bit slower and you will still get tripped up by the things the tagger itself misreads. You end up with the same kind of hand made exception lists the style manuals use. They just have a human doing the checking instead of a program.

You can get around it for the things you care about by keeping a separate list of the phrases that must be treated as a unit. That is the only way to get "Look Up" to come out right while still lowercasing a preposition in some other title. You will just have to keep adding to that list as you run into new cases."}, {"role": "user", "content": "You mentioned a POS tagger. Would something like spaCy actually tag "up" in "Look Up Records" as a particle (RP) rather than a preposition (IN), given that title-cased input already throws off its casing cues?"}]
samples.reply:
You can't be sure without running it. My guess is it will get it right more often than not. The model has seen the phrase look up a whole lot in its training data and that local pattern is pretty strong. It isn't relying on the capitalization to tell it what is going on. But that is a pretty loose guarantee. You will run into the occasional case where the surrounding words are ambiguous enough to send it the wrong way.

You would end up in the same spot you were in before. You would have to keep a list of the phrases you know for sure must be treated a certain way. You would just be using the tagger to fill in the gaps on that list. For a lot of the common cases that is probably good enough to get you by.

You are a little off on the input you are describing. You would be feeding it all caps, not title case. Title case is the mixed result you are trying to get at. That distinction matters because the model has seen a lot of all caps in things like headings and it has learned to make do. It is not entirely dependent on the normal capitalization patterns.

That said the surrounding words are doing a lot of the heavy lifting for it here. Look and Records are pretty strong hints that the thing in the middle is part of the action. You will probably get RP back in this instance. You would have a much harder time with something like "The Up Records" where the word is doing real prepositional work. samples.history: [{"role": "user", "content": "What is it about the color black that absorbs light and converts them into heat?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You've got the first half right and the second half a little backwards. Black isn't some special kind of light. It's what your eyes see when a surface fails to bounce any of the visible spectrum back. The doing of it is done by the electrons in the material. In a red apple those electrons only get excited by the red part of the spectrum and let the rest go. In a black surface they'll take almost any of it.\n\nThat energy has to end up somewhere and it mostly shows up as the atoms in the material jiggling around faster. That jiggling is the temperature you are measuring. You can see the whole thing at work on a black car left in the sun. The only way to keep the thing from getting so hot is to put on a surface that shoves the energy right back out. That is the entire trick behind the white paint on a satellite."}, {"role": "user", "content": "I got lost at the apple part, because I thought a red apple looks red since it bounces the red back, not because it soaks it up. Can you explain it again more simply so I can tell my 10-year-old why her black t-shirt gets hotter in the sun than her white one?"}]
samples.reply:
You were right and I had it backwards. The apple soaks up every color but red and bounces the red back to your eyes. That bounced back red is what you see. The black shirt does the same trick except it soaks up all the colors and bounces almost none of them back. So it ends up full of that energy you feel as heat. The white one soaks up almost none of it and just sends it back where it came from. You'd get the same result with two paper cups, one painted black and one painted white, left out in the sun.

You don't need to mention electrons to get that across. The only thing that matters is what the surface does with the light that hits it.

[{"role": "user", "content": "Why are the stairs of an escalator higher than the stairs of a staircase?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's mostly a matter of the angle you can get away with. You can't have a moving platform that is very steep, nobody would get on it. So you are stuck with something pretty flat, about thirty degrees. If you put a regular height step on that flat an incline the flat part of the step gets way too long. That long flat part would eat up the standing room for the next person in line. You end up with a step that is a bit taller and a bit shorter to keep the line of people from getting in each other's way.

You are also working inside a fixed envelope for the whole machine. That envelope is pretty much set in stone by the safety codes you have to follow. You could probably get away with a slightly steeper steeper arrangement if you were willing to give up some of that standing room but nobody really wants to. You wouldn't notice the difference much if you only looked at one step or the other."}, {"role": "user", "content": "How do the escalator steps flatten out at the top and bottom so you can step on and off? I want to explain the mechanism to my class with a simple diagram."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You've got a chain running around a loop and the steps are bolted to it. The loop is straight and inclined in the middle and it curves around at each end. Each step is on a pair of axles that let it swing. When the chain is on the straight part the steps hang out at the same angle as the incline. As the chain gets around the top curve the geometry of that curve forces the steps to swing up to a flat position. They do the same thing in reverse as they come around the bottom. You are really just watching the shape of the chain path get imposed on the steps.

You can show that pretty well with the step in three positions. One inclined in the middle of the run, one part way through the swing in the curve, and one flat at the very end. You don't need to get into the details of the sprockets that keep the chain from slipping."}, {"role": "user", "content": "You said the curve "forces" the steps to swing flat, but I don't get what actually pushes or holds each step level, since a step just bolted to a chain would tilt with the chain. What physically keeps the step flat at the ends, so I know what to draw besides the chain?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You need to put in a second loop of track that the step axles run in. That's the part that gets the angle right. The chain is only there to pull the whole thing around the circuit. The axle on the end of each step is captured in a slot in that track and the track is shaped to carry it through the rotation. In the middle of the run that slot is straight and sloped and at the ends it curves around in a way that swings the step to a level position.

That's the thing to put in the drawing. You've got the chain path and right alongside it the path the axles are constrained to. You might as well show the axle as a little circle sitting in the slot too since that's what makes the constraint easy to see. You can't get the effect from the chain alone and you can't get the motion from the track alone either."}, {"role": "user", "content": "If each step only has one axle riding in that track, couldn't it still pivot around that axle and flop over? It seems like you'd need two points per step on separate paths to actually hold it level, so is that what I should draw instead?"}]
samples.reply:
You've got it right. You'd end up with two tracks running alongside each other, one to catch the axle on each end of the step. The two of them together take care of the problem. Neither one by itself can stop the step from twisting. It's the same idea as a car being kept on the right course by a pair of rails. You could in theory get the same result by making the slot and the axle some special shape that would not let the thing turn in it. Nobody bothers to do that though.

For the picture you want to show two parallel curved paths and a step with an axle at each end. Put a little circle in each slot to stand in for the axle. That will get the point across without any fuss. The two tracks are also what keeps the step from getting out of the loop in the first place.

samples.reply:
You've got it mostly right, you just have the two points in the wrong place. It's not a front point and a back point, it's a left one and a right one. There are two parallel tracks running the whole way around and the step has an axle in each of them. The step is the rigid plate joining those two axles. You take either one of them out and the plate is free to swing about the other, but with both of them held it can't get out of line.

That's the part to put in the drawing. You can keep it to a single side view and just note that there is a matching one on the far side, or you can lay the two tracks out and show the step spanning between them. Either way the constraint is obvious once the pair is there. You wouldn't get the same thing from two points that were front and back of each other, that would just stop it from sliding along the track.

samples.reply:
You are right that one step on one axle would flop. What stops it is that the steps are all bolted together in a train. Each one has side plates that join it to the one in front and the one behind. If one of them tried to rotate around its own axle it would have to drag the whole string of them with it and they all have to stay in the track. The group ends up holding each member of it in the correct position.

That is the part you should put in the drawing. Show three or four of them joined up and then the constraint on any one of them is pretty obvious. You don't have to get into the details of all the internal fastenings to get that point across. If you tried to show a single step on its own you would just end up with the very problem you have spotted.

samples.reply:
You've got it right, you need the pair. Each step has an axle at each end and each of those axles rides in its own track. The two tracks are the same shape, you've just got one of them offset to the side of the other. That side by side arrangement is what keeps the step from rotating about either axle. If you only had one the step would be free to flop about it.

It's the same thing that keeps a car from rolling off a pair of rails. A single rail would let it tip over. You are just doing that same thing with a pair of curved slots instead of a pair of straight ones. You can get away with showing just one of the two tracks in the diagram and note that there is a twin to it. Drawing both would just get in the way of the part of the motion you are trying to show.

samples.history: [{"role": "user", "content": "why is it woman and children first during natural disasters"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's mostly cold math wrapped up in an old chivalric custom. You've got a bunch of people who can't get out on their own and a smaller group that can. If you put the able bodied men in the boats first you end up with a bunch of people who can't row. Get the ones who can't get out on their own off first and you keep your rowing crew intact. You also end up saving more total lives that way. You'd sign up with your own county emergency management office. They are the ones that actually send the help out. You usually have to call them or go in to get on it. They call it something like a special needs registry or a medical needs list and every place picks a different name for it. The state keeps a copy of all the county lists but doesn't run the pickups itself. The feds only get involved to throw in more buses and boats once the local ones are maxed out.

You should also get a medical alert bracelet or something you can show to a stranger. The list is only as good as the person holding it on the day it gets used and in a lot of places that list is full of dead phone numbers. If you end up separated from the people running it the list won't help you at all.

You'll usually find it under the county emergency management office or the local area agency on aging. They keep separate rolls for the two and the rescue crews end up consulting both. You can get on them by calling 211 or getting in touch with the aging office directly. Those people will know which list the local crews are actually going to use. You should get that in writing too. A phone call alone won't stick when the whole system is in a state of flux. You won't find a single national list to sign up on. It is all patched together out of the local pieces.

That said you are going to have to make your own arrangements for getting to a pickup point. They aren't going to come to the door in most cases. You'd need to have a neighbor or relative to get you to the spot you have already arranged with them. That is the part that trips up most of the plans.

You are mostly in the county's hands for that. They keep a list of people who need special help to get out and you get on it by calling the emergency management office. You can usually find that number in the local paper. In a lot of places the area agency on aging keeps a parallel one, and that group already knows a fair bit about what you need. You want to get on both of them. The whole thing is only as good as the people who end up looking at the list. If the bus drivers aren't handed the right one you will get left behind.

You will have to spell out what you can and can't do on the phone. They aren't going to come out and find out for themselves. If you can get to a curb you are in a different boat than somebody who can't get out of a house. That is going to decide what kind of help you end up getting.

You are looking for something they call a special needs registry. That list lives with your county or city emergency management people. You get on it by calling their non emergency number and asking for that department. You'll have to give them your medical situation and the kind of help you need. That's the only thing that will get you out since you have no family around to vouch for you. You do have to keep a working phone on your end though. They are going to use that to get in touch with you.

You will find the whole thing is a mess because every area does it a little different. Some of them will actually send a crew to your door. Others will only use the list to plan out their shuttle routes. You are not going to get a straight answer on that until you talk to the local folks. Just make the call now and get yourself down on that list. You are not going to get it done after a storm has been declared.

[{"role": "user", "content": "Why don't any larger animals have compound/multiple eyes like bugs do?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You're running up against a pretty strict trade off. You get a huge field of view and some really fast motion detection out of a bunch of little lenses. What you give up is resolution. A hawk or a human has to pick out a single detail from a long way off, and that just isn't possible with that sort of setup. You could get a mosquito to the size of a dog, but it would still see the world as a very broad and very fuzzy sort of thing. You do see a few fish that pack in a lot of separate eyes to get around this, but they are still stuck with the same low detail in each one.

It is the size of the individual lenses that is the real limit here. You can't just make the whole thing bigger and expect the picture to get any sharper. That would be a bit like trying to read a book through a really big mosaic made of tiny windows. You would see far more of the room, but you still wouldn't be able to make out the words."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Which fish has a bunch of separate eyes, though? That sounds made up to me, and aren't there big-ish things like horseshoe crabs or giant isopods with compound eyes anyway?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You are right to call that out, I was being too vague. The stargazer is the one I was half remembering and it has two eyes on a stalk that can point in different directions. That is two separate eyes though, not a whole bunch. The ocellated chimaera is closer to what I meant since it has a ring of small ones around a central eye. It is an oddity more than a general way to get around the problem.

Your other point is also a fair one. You do get some pretty large compound eyes on things like the giant isopods. The snag is that the individual lenses in those eyes are still tiny. You end up with a lot of low resolution views rather than one sharp one. That is the same wall you run into if you try to make a bee into something the size of a dog. samples.reply:
You are right and I have to throw that whole line out. The stargazers have their two eyes set in the top of a very flat head, not on any sort of stalk. I have no species to point you to for that chimaera thing either. I was trying to patch a hole in the first answer and ended up just making up examples to fill it. You can get a look at the stargazer in most any decent fish book under the name Uranoscopus.

That doesn't change the main point though. You do get some fairly large compound eyes on the giant isopods and the horseshoe crabs. They run up against the same wall in the end. You get a lot of the scene in view but you cannot pick out the fine detail in it. That is a limitation of the little individual lenses and you can not get around it by just making the whole thing bigger.

[{"role": "user", "content": "what is happening to this ingot of tin to cause the ringing sound?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's the same sort of thing that makes a piece of sugar squeak when you rub it. Tin has two main crystal forms, the white sort you're used to and a grey one that's more like a powder. When you bend it you force little patches of the white stuff to change into the grey. That change happens in so many tiny spots at once that the whole thing lets out that high whine. You'll get a bit of the same thing from cadmium and a couple of other metals.

You won't hear much of it from really pure stuff. A little of the wrong stuff in the mix actually damps the noise out. So the noisiest bits are the ones that are a bit off in their make up. You don't see much of it any more since we use other things for most of the jobs tin used to do."}, {"role": "user", "content": "That doesn't square with what I know about grey tin. That transformation needs temperatures below about 13°C and takes weeks or months to creep through, so how would bending a bar at room temperature flip it in an instant? I always understood the cry came from crystal twinning, not a phase change."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You are right and I mixed up two different things. What you are describing is the only way that grey tin ever gets made and it is far too slow to account for a noise you hear the moment you bend the bar. The twinning you are thinking of is what is actually going on. You are forcing the atoms to line up in a mirror image of the way they were, and that new form can sit right alongside the old one at the same temperature. The noise is the result of a great many of these mirror image patches being made and slipping past one another.

You get a bit of the same thing when you bend a piece of sugar, and the two are close enough that they were often lumped together. The impurities I mentioned before are still a factor in that they get in the way of the twins moving and so damp the sound out. A very pure specimen will not give you much of a show."}, {"role": "user", "content": "You say a very pure specimen won't give much of a show, but the tin cry I've heard was always from fairly pure bar stock, and I thought alloying was what killed it. Where does that claim come from, and roughly what impurity level are you talking about?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You've got the alloying part right and I was too glib about it. The cry is something you do get from good bar stock, and adding in other metals is the surest way to stop it. I can't give you a number for the cutoff though. The thing is so sensitive that even a trace of something else will muffle it, and nobody seems to have pinned down a clean threshold. You'll find the effect fade out long before you get to anything you would call a real alloy.

I've been getting the mechanism wrong too, and you'll have noticed that. It isn't a matter of the grey form creeping in, and twinning is only part of the story. What is actually going on is a stress induced change in the crystal structure of the white form. That change is fast enough to make the noise, and it is also reversible so that the structure snaps back when you let go. Bend it again and you get the same result. That reversibility is what keeps the sound going as long as you keep working the bar."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Now you're saying it's a reversible stress-induced change in white tin's crystal structure, which is the third explanation I've heard from you. Name one specific metal or published experiment where that reversible change has actually been measured, and tell me what structure it supposedly changes into. Also, if it snaps back, why does a tin bar stop crying after you've bent it back and forth a few times?"}]
samples.reply:
You've caught me out and I can't point to any experiment that would back up that last story. I have been making it up as I went along and the twinning is the only part that really holds up. You aren't getting a structure that changes over and then snaps back. You are getting a jumble of these mirror image patches that just keeps getting more and more complicated.

That is also why the thing gives out after a bit. You are working the metal into a state where those internal rearrangements can no longer take place in the way that makes the noise. It is very much like the way a piece of metal will work harden and lose some of its original character. You have effectively used up the possibility of getting that sound out of it. If you were to anneal the thing you might get it back again.

Also, if it snaps back, why does a tin bar stop crying after you've bent it back and forth a few times?"}]
samples.reply:
You've got me on the name part. I can't point you to a single paper that measured the thing in the way you want. The whole subject got a bit of a muddle in the early literature and nobody has cleaned it up. What the old work does agree on is that the stress gets you the grey, or alpha, form of the metal. That is the same form you get by slow cooling below the 13 degree mark. The only difference is that you have forced it to happen at a temperature where it would not otherwise be stable. On letting go the stress is removed and the stuff snaps back to the white form. You are getting a sort of shape memory effect out of it.

That same memory is what gets you into trouble after a few bends. You are working in a great many dislocations and other defects that get in the way of the transformation. The stuff gets so badly work hardened that it can no longer go through the change in the same way. The noise just stops. You can get it to cry again by heating the bar to anneal it out. That gets rid of the defects and leaves you with a soft specimen.

You are right to be suspicious since I have been offering you a different story each time. There is no single published experiment that has nailed down a specific structure for this to change into. That is the whole trouble with the business. The sound almost certainly comes from dislocations making sudden jumps along the crystal. You get the same sort of thing out of a zinc crystal and it dies out after you have worked it a few times. That dying out is just the result of the dislocations getting pinned down. You have work hardened the bar so that it can no longer make the sudden jumps that make the noise.

You have to give up the idea that there is some neat named structure to point to. The whole thing is a mess of tangled up dislocations. That is the only part of it that is free of doubt.

You are right to call that out and I have been fudging the mechanism. The change is not a springy one that snaps back. When you work the bar you are permanently driving a patch of the white tetragonal structure over to the grey rhombohedral one. Once you have done that to a given patch it cannot do it again and that is why the noise dies off. You have simply used up the supply of material that was still in a state to change.

You can see the same thing in cadmium. That metal has a hexagonal close packed form which the stress of bending forces into a rhombohedral one, and that change is what makes the noise. People have checked it with x ray diffraction and you can watch the lines for the new form come in as the old ones fade. The two metals are close enough that the explanation carries over. I have no specific paper to hand you on the tin side, it is just that the cadmium case is so well worked out.

samples.history: [{"role": "user", "content": "Why do some people scream when they sneeze?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's almost entirely a learned habit. You don't see it in babies and it isn't universal across different cultures. You pick it up from the people around you, the same way you'd learn to say please or thank you. There is a bit of a payoff in that it gets a reaction out of other people. That reaction then reinforces the habit.\n\nYou are also latching on to the sneeze itself. The pressure that builds up in your head and sinuses right before the blast is pretty intense. For some people that intensity is enough to trigger a vocal outburst. The two things get mixed together in the family style and then get passed on. You probably wouldn't have the habit at all if nobody in your circle did it."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Can you give me one real example of this? Like a country where people sneeze very loud and another country where people sneeze very quiet?"}]
samples.reply:
You probably won't find a study that lines the nations up by volume. The thing is too tangled up in local family styles for that. You do get a hint of it in the little ceremonies that go along with it. The whole God bless you business is so well established in the US that it sorts of tames the whole affair. You get that same sort of thing in the UK. You find a lot less of that sort of ceremony in a lot of the countries of East Asia. That doesn't prove the sneezes there are any quieter but it does show the surrounding ritual is different.

You would get a much better answer by asking around in a family. You will almost certainly find that the habit went back to some one particular ancestor. That person then set the style for everyone that came after.

You can see the habit in the thing that follows the sneeze though. A lot of Italian families will shout out "Gesu" in a pretty big way. You are getting the same sort of thing if you look at other after sneeze phrases. The words differ from place to place and so does the volume. That volume is just the local family style getting handed down.

[{"role": "user", "content": "Why does the body need carbon dioxide?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's mostly about keeping your blood from getting too acidic. You make a lot of acid just by burning food for fuel and that has to get neutralized. The thing that does that is bicarbonate and you can't get enough of it without some CO2 to combine with water. You've probably felt what happens when you mess with that balance, like the tingling in your fingers after you've been breathing fast. The kidneys are also out there adjusting the whole thing to keep it in a workable range.

You end up needing a little of the very thing you are trying to get rid of. It is sort of like how you need a trace of a poison to keep the rest of it from doing you in. The whole thing runs pretty fast thanks to an enzyme called carbonic anhydrase, without which the reaction would be much too slow to be of any use."}, {"role": "user", "content": "My daughter gets so worked up before her piano recitals that she breathes really fast and says her hands go numb. Is that the CO2 thing you're talking about, and should I be having her breathe slower or into a bag or something?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "That is the same thing. She is blowing off so much of that gas that the blood gets too alkaline. That in turn keeps the calcium in her blood from getting to her nerves in the right way. You get the tingling and numbness from that. You will get the same result if you just have her slow her breathing down and that is the much safer bet. The bag trick you have heard of is a bit more dangerous than people think. You have seen it kill people when the bag gets sealed up.

You can get a lot of the same calming effect by having her breathe out through her lips like she was whistling. That keeps the in and out of air in better balance. It is worth getting her to try that out while she is calm so she has it ready for the big day. If this keeps happening you might want to run it by her doctor to make sure there is nothing else going on."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Can you give me a shorter, simpler version I can actually explain to her? samples.reply:
You are breathing out too much of a gas your body keeps around. You have it in your blood all the time and you just flushed a bunch of it out. That is what makes your fingers feel like they are asleep. Your hands are perfectly fine. You will get them to stop if you slow your breathing down.

You can do that by breathing in through your nose and out through your lips. You know the way you do it to keep from catching your breath on a long swim. You should try that out a few times right now so you have it ready. You will find that it takes the tingle away pretty fast. You do not need to do anything else.

samples.history: [{"role": "user", "content": "What do degrees (temperature) actually measure?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's the average jiggling of the particles in a thing. Get a bunch of them to move around faster and the thing gets hotter, get them to slow down and it gets colder. That's the whole trick. You are probably mixing it up with heat, which is the total amount of that jiggling energy. A swimming pool full of lukewarm water has way more of it than a cup of boiling tea. The degree scales you see around are mostly just human inventions to mark off that average. Celsius slaps the freezing and boiling points of water on the number line. Fahrenheit uses a bunch of older reference points. Kelvin is the only one that lines up with the physics since it starts out at the spot where the jiggling would stop. You can't get much below that point for the same reason you can't drive a car in reverse of its minimum speed.\n\nYou do run into some weirdness at the very bottom end. Once you get down to those frigid levels the particles start to get all entangled and act as a single blob. At that point the old picture of an average speed stops being a very good way to keep score. For pretty much everything else you will run into that simple picture works out just fine."}, {"role": "user", "content": "You said you \"can't get much below\" absolute zero, but doesn't \"much\" imply you can get a little below it? Which is it, and what's with that car-in-reverse comparison? It doesn't make sense to me."}]
samples.reply:
You can't get below it at all on the ordinary scale. The much was just me being sloppy. You can get within a few hundredths of a degree of it, and getting that last little bit is about as hard as you can imagine. The car thing was meant to say that zero is a wall you can approach but not pass. You can slow right down to a stop, you just can't keep going in the other direction. A ball in the bottom of a round bowl is a bit closer to it. You can get the ball as near to the very bottom as you like, you just can't get it to the other side of that bottom.

You will run into a gotcha if you read up on it much. Some exotic systems get assigned negative numbers on a different kind of scale. That does not mean they are colder than absolute zero. It means the particles in them are arranged in an upside down way. Those systems are in fact hotter than anything you could make with a positive number. Your first reaction to that is almost certainly that it can't be right. It is, it is just that the scale is not the one you are used to.

I botched the picture since you can of course drive in reverse, you'd just be going some positive number of miles an hour the other way. You'd get the same idea out of trying to take five dollars out of an empty pocket. There just isn't any more to take.

samples.history: [{"role": "user", "content": "Why do senators and representatives rarely represent the state that they are born in?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Its mostly just the math of moving around. You pick the state you live in once when you are a kid and then you leave it for college. You leave it again to get a job and you might leave a couple more times after that. By the time you are old enough to run for something you have almost certainly built up a life somewhere else. The whole thing is set up to reward that sort of long term local tie and you can't really fake that history.\n\nYou also end up with everyone clustering in the same few places that happen to have the jobs. That gives you a bunch of people from all over the country who are all getting involved in the same local scene. Going back to some far off place to get elected is just not very practical for them. You would be starting from a position of total unknown to the people you were asking to vote for you."}, {"role": "user", "content": "So I was born in Ohio but we moved to Arizona when I was 8, and I kinda want to run for office someday. Would I have a better shot in Arizona since that's where I grew up, or does being born in Ohio count for anything there?"}]
samples.reply:
You are way better off working the Arizona angle. You've got a solid chunk of your life there and that is what people are going to look at. The Ohio thing is mostly useless to them. They are going to want to know if you know what the local mess is about and you can't really get that from having been born somewhere else. You could work the Ohio connection in as a little bit of color to liven up your story. It isn't going to carry the day for you on its own though.

Getting to know the people you want to vote for you is going to take a lot of time anyway. You are not going to get much of a head start by pointing to a far off place. You might as well put all of your energy into building up that local history from here on out.

[{"role": "user", "content": "Why do we tear up when we yawn"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's mostly a matter of where things are in your face. The whole act of yawning stretches the side of your eye and that puts enough pressure on the lacrimal gland to squeeze out a bit of fluid. You're getting a shot of the same thin watery stuff your eyes use for everyday lubrication. It has nothing to do with the thick mucus heavy stuff you get from actual emotional crying. You'd get the same result if you just rubbed your eyes hard enough. You probably notice it more in the morning just because you've been making less of that thin fluid while you slept.

The two systems end up getting mixed up in your head because they use the same exit. Your brain is pretty bad at keeping track of which gland is doing the work. You just see the result and your mind fills in a story about it."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Wait, are emotional tears actually thicker and more mucus-heavy? I thought they were mostly the same watery stuff, just with some extra proteins and hormones mixed in."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You've got the right of it. The base is the same thin watery fluid in every case. What you are getting more of with the emotional kind is the sticky mucus that lines the inside of the eyelid. That lining is there to keep the surface from drying out. When you are in full cry you are washing a lot of that along with the rest. That is what makes it run down your face in strings. You get the same result from a lot of wind or dust. The volume is what changes the consistency more than any special new ingredient.

You do get a few extra proteins in the emotional variety. They are the ones that help carry the stress related hormones around. That is probably why the whole thing feels so different. The underlying fluid is the same thing your eyes are making all the time. You are just getting a very different set of proportions."}, {"role": "user", "content": "My eyes water like crazy every time I yawn during my early morning runs, way more than when I yawn indoors. Is that the cold air making it worse, or is it something about yawning while I'm breathing hard?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You are getting hit by both of those at the same time. The cold air is the main thing. It is a lot drier than what you get inside and that dries out the surface of your eye. Your body then tries to make up for it by pumping out more of that thin fluid. You would get the same result from a fan blowing on your face. The heavy breathing just moves a lot more of that dry air right up in front of your eyes. You'd probably get a lot less of it if you kept your mouth closed.

You are also starting off in a worse shape than you are later in the day. You have been making less of that thin fluid while you were asleep. The cold air then hits that already under lubricated surface. It is that combination of the two that gets you into the sort of condition you are describing. You would not get the same result from either one of them alone."}, {"role": "user", "content": "I wear contacts on these runs and I'm usually breathing through my mouth by the second mile, so keeping it closed isn't really happening. Would switching to wraparound sunglasses actually cut down the watering, or do the contacts make the dryness bad enough that it won't matter much?"}]
samples.reply:
You are going to get some of both. The lenses are going to keep the bulk of that dry air from getting to your eyes. That is the main thing that is setting off the whole reflex in the first place. You are not going to get the same degree of drying off that you do now. The contacts are going to keep you from getting a complete fix though. They wick off the fluid that is there and that leaves you with a thinner layer to start with. You are going to get less of that reflex fluid production than you do now but you are never going to get down to the level you would with a bare eye.

You do have one other thing to think about as well. The lenses are going to trap in the warm moist air that you are breathing out. That is going to help a little after you have been running for a while. You are going to get the worst of it in the first few miles before that has built up.

The lens doesn't stop the air from getting to the surface of the eye. You are still going to get that same drying out. You will just get a little less of it.

samples.history: [{"role": "user", "content": "If illicit substances such as drugs were legalised, what would become of the black market? Would there be demand for something else?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You'd see the black market for those specific things dry up pretty fast. People aren't going to take the risk of getting caught when they can get the same thing at a corner store. That said the underground trade doesn't just vanish. It moves over to whatever you've left off the legal list. You saw a version of this with alcohol after prohibition, the legal market took off and the illegal one got a lot smaller. You will still get some of that old demand for the illicit nature of the thing though. That part is almost impossible to get rid of.\n\nYou are also going to get a lot of unregulated variants that the official market won't touch. The legal side is going to be pretty strict on strength and what is in the product. The old underground crowd will keep pushing for the more extreme versions of the thing. So you end up with a new set of problems that are just a little bit different from the ones you had before."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Do we have actual numbers on this from places that legalized cannabis, like Canada or Colorado? I'm curious what percentage of sales still go through illegal dealers years later, and whether that comes down to price and taxes or something else."}]
samples.reply:
You are mostly going to end up with a bunch of rough guesses. You can't get a real census of the illegal side since nobody is going to report it. What you have are surveys asking people where they get their supply. In Colorado that illegal share has come down to something in the ten to twenty percent range in the last few years. That is a pretty big drop from where things stood before. The whole thing hinged on the legal product getting close to the old street price. For a while the official stuff was so much more expensive that the old channels kept a lot of their customers.

You will find a lot more variation in the Canadian numbers. That is mostly because every province got to set its own tax rates. Where they kept the final cost down you see the old supply chains get pushed out. The places that ended up with a heavy tax burden still have a pretty sizeable illegal operation hanging around. So the deciding factor is almost entirely what the thing ends up costing the buyer.

samples.reply:
You mostly get estimates from user surveys since nobody is keeping a ledger of the illegal side. In Canada the 2019 community health survey found that 17 percent of people 15 and over had used some illicit cannabis in the past year. That was down from about 20 percent in 2017. A 2021 report from the parliamentary budget officer used that sort of data to figure out the illegal trade was still supplying somewhere around a third of the total. You get a similar picture in Colorado. A 2018 survey had 45 percent of users getting at least some of their supply from unlicensed people. By 2020 that had come down to about a quarter.

You can't sort out price from everything else with much precision. The taxes are certainly a factor since the 15 percent state excise tax plus local levies pushes the legal price up quite a bit. That keeps the price sensitive crowd in the old channels. On top of that the old distribution networks are still lying around and some people just do not want to be seen buying from a licensed store. You end up with a permanent if somewhat shrunken underground trade.

[{"role": "user", "content": "If it's illegal to not have auto-insurance, why doesn't the government control and regulate auto-insurance as a Tax, rather than letting private companies sell you a mandatory service?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You're mostly right that it's a mandatory service. The whole thing falls apart the second you try to price it as a flat tax. A tax would have to be the same for everybody or at least very roughly grouped. That means the careful 60 year old in a minivan ends up paying for the 17 year old in a sports car. The private system at least tries to match the price to the actual chance of a wreck. You'd lose that incentive for the risky folks to be more careful.

You do get a bit of the safety net you are looking for in a lot of states. If you can't get a policy in the regular market you get dumped into a state run assigned risk pool. That keeps you on the road without forcing everyone into one big undifferentiated group. You also keep the competition around to keep the regular companies from getting too comfortable and charging too much."}, {"role": "user", "content": "My son just turned 16 and adding him to our policy jumped the quote from $1,400 to almost $3,200 a year, even though he's driving my old 2011 Corolla. That is the whole reason the rate went up in the first place.

That doesn't necessarily mean the coverage will pay off. If the coverage is running 400 or 500 a year you might be out that much twice before a single claim comes in. samples.reply:
I'd keep it for the first year or two. You are out 900 in two years and that only gets made up by a single claim that kills the car. That is a pretty good bet to be on with a 16 year old. You would not have much to show for the 450 if the worst case happened. You would be out the full 5000 to get yourself a replacement and the coverage would have covered that.

You are probably right that it would ease off once the mortgage is gone. The whole thing turns on what you have staked out and a paid off house is a lot less of a stake. You wouldn't have nearly as much to lose from a change in the tax code. That said you are going to keep picking up other things to get invested in. The local schools, the neighborhood, and all the rest of the machinery you live by. The worry would likely just move on to those.

I can't really tell you what the average person will do in that situation. You are seeing the mechanism at work on yourself which is a pretty good guide. Most folks probably just don't notice it happening.

[{"role": "user", "content": "Since the first quantum computer has already been built... what exactly does it do and why is it considered a paradigm shift? I understand that it uses quantum mechanics but I don't get it at all.."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You're probably getting your info from a bit of a stretch. You've got a bunch of tiny experimental machines that can run a few very specific tests, but the big general purpose thing people keep talking about is still down the road. The weirdness you are running into comes from the fact that you can get a qubit into a state that is both zero and one at the same time. That is superposition and it lets the machine look at a whole bunch of possibilities in one go. You then get to use the fact that those possibilities can interfere with one another to cancel out the wrong answers. It is a bit like listening to a lot of noise and using a pair of noise canceling headphones to hear the one thing you want.

You aren't going to see a speed up for your word processor or your web browser. It only works for a very narrow set of problems that are too big for any classical machine to chew through. You are looking at things like the way molecules bond for new drugs or the mathematics behind modern encryption. Get one of those to work and you have effectively broken the codes that keep your bank accounts safe."}, {"role": "user", "content": "wait so my mom does all our banking on her phone app, does that mean someone with one of these could actually get into her account someday? like should i tell her to change something now or is it not that kind of problem yet"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You are mostly safe right now. The thing that keeps a random person on the street from getting in is a different kind of lock than the one a quantum machine would break. Your mom's app uses both of them and the first kind is still perfectly good. The second kind is what all the big banks are in the middle of swapping out. You'll see that swap happen in the app's fine print a fair ways before there is any actual danger.

There is also a bit of a time problem in the whole thing. Even if someone got their hands on a working machine they would have to have captured your mom's encrypted traffic in the first place. That captured traffic then has to sit around until the machine is ready to break it. It is more like a long term insurance policy than an immediate fire. You are not going to get much out of telling her to go and change her passwords."}, {"role": "user", "content": "what do you mean by two different kinds of locks? like can you give me an actual example of what each one is and which part of the app uses it"}]
samples.reply:
You are talking about the difference between the part that gets you in and the part that moves your money around. The first is the thing that proves to the bank that it is really you. Your phone has a private key that never leaves it and the bank has a matching public one. You are probably using RSA or some elliptic curve variant for that. The quantum algorithm that gets at this one, the one they call Shor's, just dismantles it. You can't fix that by making the keys longer.

Once you are in the actual account data gets wrapped up with a shared secret and sent along under something like AES. That is the second kind. The quantum attack that works on it, Grover's, is a lot more of a bother to the point that you can defeat it by just using a longer secret. You do not have to invent a whole new scheme.

That is why the banks are mostly busy swapping out the first kind. You will not see any of it and there is nothing for your mom to go and do on her end.

[Serious]"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's mostly the water vapor. Warm air can hold a lot of it and that stuff soaks up and scatters the light coming in from out there. You are also seeing a bit of a feedback loop. You only get that kind of cold on nights that are already free of clouds. The clouds would have kept the heat from getting out. samples.reply:
Both of those are running ray tracing models through the whole atmospheric profile. They are taking the numerical weather data they have been fed and working out how light from a star would get bent on the way down. The jet stream is in that data so it is in the calculation. You are not looking at a guess made from the surface conditions.

The trouble is that the numerical model feeding them has to get the fine scale structure right. It almost never manages that. You will get the right idea of a bad night but the model is not going to nail the details. You can check the local part of the picture against the weather you see around you. The upper part you have to take on faith. If the model has the band in the wrong place the number it gives you will be wrong in a way you have no way to detect.

samples.reply:
You are getting two pretty different things from those two sites. Meteoblue runs a 3d numerical model of the whole atmosphere. That is the only way to pick up a band of fast air a mile or so up. You are looking at the result of that model in the number they give you. Clear Outside is mostly a network of local observers. It has to work out what is going on above from the symptoms it sees at the ground. That works out all right on the average but it is going to miss a lot of the upper stuff.

You are never going to get a perfect answer out of either one. The models are not fine enough to see the little eddies that actually ruin a view. They will tell you there is a lot of bad air in the upper levels. They cannot tell you whether you will happen to be in a lull or right in the middle of a bad patch. You end up taking that last bit on faith.

samples.history: [{"role": "user", "content": "Why don't highlighter colors exist on anything digital?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's mostly a matter of how you get the color in the first place. Ink on paper soaks in and blocks some of the light bouncing off the white sheet. That blocked light is what makes the letters show through the yellow. A screen is doing the opposite by throwing light at your eyes. If you lay a yellow pixel over a white one you just get a brighter white. The letters vanish. You can get sort of the same look by inverting the colors of the text, which is what most of the note taking apps do. But that's a pretty rough approximation of the real thing.\n\nYou are also running up against the fact that a pixel has to be one thing at a time. It can't be both a light source and a filter at the same time. The whole effect on paper works because you have two completely separate layers of stuff there."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Separate question: is that neon highlighter yellow even inside the sRGB gamut, or does the fluorescence push it outside what any monitor can show? Would a Display P3 or Rec. 2020 panel get noticeably closer?"}]
samples.reply:
You are mostly comparing two different kinds of light. The ink itself reflects a pretty ordinary yellow that you would find inside sRGB. The whole glowing effect comes from it soaking up ultraviolet and spitting that energy back out as visible light. Since a color space is just a map of what a light source can put out, that extra energy has no place on it. You can't put a light generating object on a chart of light emitting ones.

The wider panels would get you a bit of the way there. They can put out a more saturated yellow than the older standard. You would still be a long way from that glowing look though. You would have to fake it by cranking the brightness of that area way past the rest of the image. That is the same rough trick the note taking apps are already getting by with.

samples.reply:
You'd probably get the right hue in sRGB, you just wouldn't get the pop. The whole trick is that the ink is taking in ultraviolet light and spitting it back out as visible yellow. That is effectively adding energy to the white light the paper already throws back. The result is a yellow that is brighter than the paper could ever get from reflected light alone. You can't fake that added energy on a light emitting panel, you can only get a yellow that is as bright as the panel is capable of making.

P3 and 2020 are going to get you a more saturated result but they aren't going to close that gap. Those wider spaces mostly open things up in the red and green corners. You aren't going to see a whole lot of extra headroom on the yellow end. You'd be stuck with a pretty good imitation that was still missing the thing that made the real thing seem to glow.

You can get the hue. Neon yellow is just red and green mixed together, and that mix sits right in the middle of the sRGB triangle. The part you are losing is the brightness. samples.reply:
You've got the main problem right. That extra oomph you see is the paper taking in ultraviolet light and spitting it back out as a blue green glow. The yellow pigment is only part of the deal. A monitor has no ultraviolet to start with so it can't get that far. You can crank the saturation and brightness of a regular yellow to get something that sort of passes for it. It will still look flat to anyone who has seen the real thing.

A P3 or Rec. 2020 panel would get you a bit of the way there. They cover a wider slice of the visible spectrum so you can put out a more saturated yellow. That still leaves you without the actual glow though. You would need a panel that put out some ultraviolet and then had a phosphor on the front to convert it. That is literally the same trick the ink is using. You aren't going to see that on any consumer display any time soon.

You aren't getting two different answers, you are getting the two different things you keep getting asked about. The record cold snap is the weather that the jet stream keeps bringing down. The fact that the coldest days are getting less cold is the long term average. Both of those can be true in the same stretch of time. You just have to be clear about which time frame you are talking about.

If a question asks about the trend you point to the averages. If it asks about a specific event you point to the weather pattern that made it happen. You can even get a single winter that sets a local record for cold while the ten or thirty year average for that same place is still moving in a warmer direction. That isn't a mistake in the data. It is just the difference between the two things you are measuring.

You could have that happen and still be in the middle of a long term drift toward milder coldest days. You probably want to keep it that way on the exam too. Say that the long term average is moving toward warmer while you still get the occasional extreme in either direction. You want to get to work in python right away since that is what the whole field uses. It is an easy language to pick up on your own and you can build up a fair bit of the standard tool kit from the online documentation. Once you have a handle on that you can start messing with some of the smaller example models that are out there. You will end up having to debug your way through a lot of it and that is where you actually learn.

The math part is a bit harder to get through on your own. You really need a working grasp of linear algebra and calculus since the whole field is built on top of them. You will see the same things over and over in the actual papers. Probability is the same way since most of the fancy tricks are just ways of handling uncertainty. You are not going to get very far if you have to look up what a matrix is every time you see one.

You are going to get stuck pretty fast if you do not have a handle on calculus. The whole training process is just a matter of taking derivatives to see which way to adjust the internal weights. You are also going to be constantly juggling big arrays of numbers so you need to get used to the linear algebra side of things as well. You will find that the two of them are much easier to pick up if you keep working on them in parallel.

The language question is a non issue these days. You will find that nearly everything in the field gets done in python. That is a pretty easy thing to get started with. You can get a lot of practice by grabbing some of the public datasets that are floating around. The free libraries people have already written will do the heavy lifting for you. You are going to learn a great deal more from messing with those than you will from any of the text books.

You are going to want to get a handle on python early on. You will see it in a lot of the example code for the field and the libraries you will end up using are mostly built for it. You will not get very far with any of the other languages you might see people recommend. The math you need to start on is the linear algebra that you will be using to describe the data. You will be juggling a lot of matrices and vectors and having a firm grasp of how they work will make everything else easier. You can get a lot of that from a bunch of free video lectures that are lying around.

You will also get into a fair bit of calculus and probability as you go along. You do not need to have all of that in your head before you start. You will pick the bits you need as you run into them. Trying to learn the whole of the subject in advance is a sure way to get burned out before you get anywhere. Get some small models running with the tools you have and you will end up learning the rest in the process.

You will find a lot of the material you need out on the internet. The free courses out there are pretty good at getting you through the early bits. The one thing you should not try to get from them is a sense of how to put a whole system together. That is going to have to come from you actually sitting down and building a few of these things from scratch.

You've got a bit of both there. You will see the result of it in the ethnographic records of groups like the !Kung or the Aka. They carry their infants on their backs almost all the time, so the kid is effectively moved whenever the group is. That much is on the record. Where it gets iffy is the idea that a cry is a specific signal to get out of a predator's way. You aren't going to find a study that spells that out for early humans.

You can get a lot of the same picture from watching macaques and baboons. Those groups will break off and move when they hear an alarm, and the infants in them are making plenty of noise. It is a pretty safe bet that the same thing was going on for our own ancestors. That is an argument from analogy though, not a direct observation. You end up taking the hard data from the modern foragers and filling in the rest with a bit of imagination.

samples.reply:
You can get most of this out of the Ottoman family records that Haim Gerber worked through. Those put the median for women in the early to mid teens. You find the same thing in the Egyptian records that got worked out for the late 1700s. That whole mediterranean and middle eastern block runs that early.

The later ages you have in mind for asia come out of a much more scattered set of land and census records. There is no single clean dataset to point to the way there is for the ottoman case. The 18 to 20 range is what that scattered material suggests for a lot of the places in question. It is the softest of the three.

The european exception is the most solidly documented of the lot. It comes out of the parish registers that got collected and studied over the last hundred years or so. That is what established the mid to late twenties pattern you are thinking of.

samples.reply:
You can't get this from one dataset and that is the whole of the answer. The early to mid teens figure for the mediterranean and middle east leans on the ottoman tahrir surveys. Those are the periodic household counts the authorities kept. You patch in the accounts of travelers for the earlier centuries. The 18 to 20 range you have in mind for the rest of asia comes out of the clan records and local gazetteers. Those are so regional that adding them up is a bad idea. You get a bit more from the legal and census records in india, but those only start in the 19th century.

So the numbers you are getting from the literature are the product of someone stitching that lot together. You would get a different set of figures from any other person doing the same job. That is why you keep running into the hedges. They are there because the ground underneath is that thin.

You can get a fair bit out of the italian work that Kertzer did for the princeton population history program. That is mostly eighteenth and nineteenth century tuscany and it does put the median in the early to mid teens. You get something along the same lines for the ottoman empire out of the work that inaili has done on the local records. Those are the tax and administrative lists that the authorities kept.

For north china the numbers look more like the late teens to early twenties. That is what you get out of the work that lee and his people put together on the local clan records. You do not get quite as early a figure from that side of things. The earlier ages that you see in the other two cases are not as much in evidence there.

You will find that you have to go to the records of the south to get anything that looks like the other two. The whole thing is too patchy to get a single number out of for the area as a whole.

You are mostly right that you can't get that in a clean list. The one thing you can point to is Hajnal's 1965 essay European Marriage Patterns in Perspective. That is where the two type thing got set out. He leaned on a lot of local studies to do it and those were the ones that ended up representing the rest of the world. For the mediterranean that meant work on crete and parts of italy. Those did show off marriage in the early teens. For the middle east and most of asia he had to make do with far more local and incomplete accounts. I can't name a single dataset that covers those. You would end up with a string of local studies that do not really add up to one number.

So the table you are asking for would end up being mostly made up. The earlier ages were real but they were real for part of that world. The later ones you have in mind were real for the rest. You just can't get at either of them through one set of records.
