[{"role": "user", "content": "If DNA is the blueprint for creating enzymes that synthesize DNA, how did DNA first come about?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "You've got the loop right and it is a real puzzle. The working guess is that the first version of it didn't use DNA at all. RNA can do both of the jobs you're describing, it holds information and it can speed up chemical reactions. So you could have a population of self copying RNA molecules that got more and more complicated over time. At some point that system probably split the two jobs off to DNA and proteins because those turned out to be better at them. You'd end up with the arrangement you see in every living thing today.

That said we still don't know the details of that hand off. Nobody has actually watched a set of RNA molecules do it in the lab. There are a few other candidates that have gotten some play, like systems based on simple peptides, but none of them has the same kind of supporting evidence. You are almost certainly looking at the end result of a long and mostly lost process of trial and error."}, {"role": "user", "content": "My daughter's asking for a real example of RNA actually speeding up a reaction like an enzyme does. Is there a specific one in living things today she could look up for her science project?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "For the project the ribosome is probably your best bet. The part of it that actually joins two amino acids together is an RNA molecule, not a protein. That reaction is called peptide bond formation and it is how every protein gets made. If she looks up peptidyl transferase she will find that the active site is made of rRNA. You can also point out that this is in bacteria, plants, and animals, so it is not some rare oddity.

If she wants something that looks more like the classic enzyme and substrate setup, RNase P is good. In bacteria an RNA part of that enzyme cuts a precursor tRNA molecule into a usable form. You can get the RNA by itself and it will still do the cutting. That is about as clear a case of RNA acting as a catalyst as you are going to find. The one wrinkle is that in some of our own cells the job has been taken over by a protein, so the bacterial version is the one to show."}, {"role": "user", "content": "You said the RNA part of RNase P still does the cutting even when it's taken out by itself. How did scientists figure that out, and is there a name or experiment she could mention in her project?"}]
samples.reply:
The whole trick was a matter of getting the two parts apart. You purify the enzyme out of the bacteria and then use chemical tricks to strip off the protein. You end up with the RNA all by itself and you give it the same tRNA it would normally act on. It still gets the job done. Do the same thing with the protein alone and you get nothing. That's the test that showed the RNA was the real worker.

What you are mostly getting from the top is the noise that has got out of their room by other means. The walls that rise from the slab, the holes for the pipes, and the duct work all act as leaky paths for the sound. Those routes are much better at getting noise up than down. You are also picking up quite a bit of it through the little gaps at the top of your walls. The room below is far more completely sealed off from you in that way.

You could get a pretty fair test by listening to a loud radio in the room below. You will get a very different and much weaker result than you get from the same thing done in the room above. That is the indirect routes at work and they are the whole of the explanation.

You are right to leave that part out. You can't actually prove that the trade picked out people for speed. Nobody kept records of who they chose and why. You are left with a group of people who shared a region and then someone decided that region must have been selected for. That is just a story that got dressed up as a fact.

You do have one thing you can measure. Certain groups in West and Central Africa have a higher share of the fast twitch muscle fibers that you need for a sprint. [{"role": "user", "content": "Why do some companies have different names for different countries? Like Lynx/Axe or Asda/Walmart"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's mostly that a name carries a bunch of baggage you can't easily shake. Axe in the US got locked into this party animal image for teenage boys. They couldn't just reposition that for the UK without trashing the whole thing they'd built up stateside. Lynx let them start from scratch with a slicker, more adult image. It's usually a lot cheaper to launch a new name than to fight off an old one.

You get the opposite situation with Asda. Walmart bought the chain and kept the local name because that name already had the trust of the people who shopped there. Slapping the Walmart label on it would have scared off a lot of that existing customer base. They do the same thing in a bunch of other countries, using names that the local shoppers already know.

You also run into the fact that you can't always get the same trademark in every place. Somebody else is often already using it. That forces you to pick a different one whether you like it or not."}, {"role": "user", "content": "I sell online and get a few orders from Canada and Australia now. Do I need to register my business name as a trademark over there too, or is my US one enough for now?"}]
samples.reply:
You're going to get nothing out of the US one. These things are strictly territorial. That registration in Washington has no legal effect in Toronto or Sydney. Some other person could get the same name registered there and you'd have no standing to stop them.

You do have a little bit of a leg to stand on in both of those places. They both give you some rights just from the fact that you've started using the name. You've got to be able to prove when that first happened though. Keep a careful record of your very first sales and any advertising you've done. If you ever have to fight for the name that paper trail is going to be your only friend.

You probably don't need to run out and get a full registration in both places right away. That gets to be a pretty good bit of money to spend on a few orders. You'd be better off keeping an eye on the situation and getting in there if the sales start to look like they are going to stick.

samples.reply:
You are right that the bigger chunk has more of the stuff in it. You are just comparing two different sized chunks. The number on the front is for one serving and the company gets to pick what one serving is. They will often print a smaller serving on the family size. So you end up with a 30 gram serving on the big bag and a 50 gram one on the little bag.

Say the stuff in the bag has 1 gram of that oil in every 100 grams of chips. Your 30 gram serving from the big bag has 0.3 of a gram in it. That gets written down as zero. The 50 gram serving from the little bag has 0.5 of a gram in it. That is the first amount they are forced to print out. You are looking at two different sized samples of the same thing.

You can check the ingredient list to see if you are getting the same product. If you see partially hydrogenated oil in both of them you know the oil is in there. That list does not get to use the same fudging. You will run into the same sort of trick with a lot of the other numbers on the box.

samples.reply:
There wasn't so much a signed agreement as there was a private chat. Roosevelt got together with the king, Ibn Saud, on a warship in the Suez Canal in 1945. You remember the little story and then have to figure out what it was trying to tell you.

You can usually tell which you have got by seeing whether you can strip the rhyme away and still have the instruction left. If you do that to the second one you are left with pretty much nothing.

samples.reply: That name came from the best speed the network could reach in the most favorable conditions. In a strong signal pocket you might get a few megabits per second. Out in the field the same network usually fell back to the older 3G rate. Your phone simply kept showing the 4G label that the carrier had assigned to it.
